title: Rise of Militarism in Japan (1919–1937)
tagline: Party government and its collapse, the militarist takeover, Manchuria and the invasion of China.

overview.intro: Japan entered the twentieth century as the only major non-Western industrial power, and by the 1930s its government had passed from civilian party cabinets to military rule. This unit traces the growth of Japanese nationalism and imperialism from 1919, the party government of the 1920s and the reasons it failed, the seizure of Manchuria in 1931, the militarist government of the 1930s and the invasion of China that began in 1937.

blocks.text: Japan emerged from the First World War with expanded interests, taking the German concessions in Shandong at the peace conference and pressing for the racial equality clause that was refused, a rebuff that hardened opinion in Japan that the western powers would not treat it as an equal. In 1910 Japan had annexed Korea, and the following decade saw the consolidation of a position in southern Manchuria through the South Manchuria Railway, the Kwantung lease and the presence of troops, alongside the twenty-one demands placed on China in 1915.

Nationalism at home was shaped by a state that promoted loyalty through education and the emperor system, and by a political culture in which the military reported to the emperor rather than to the cabinet. That constitutional ambiguity mattered: the war minister and navy minister had to be serving officers, so a cabinet could be brought down simply by their resignation, and the armed forces therefore possessed a permanent lever over civilian government.

blocks.text: The 1920s saw the practice of government passing to cabinets formed by the parties that commanded a majority in the Diet, beginning with Hara in 1918, the first commoner prime minister. The party governments pursued the Washington naval agreement, which limited naval construction, and a foreign policy described as positive diplomacy, and in 1925 the franchise was extended to all men over twenty-five. The same year the Peace Preservation Law allowed the arrest of those who sought to alter the kokutai or the system of private property, which gave the authorities a weapon against the left while the vote was being widened.

Party government rested on support that was fragile. The zaibatsu industrial combines funded the parties, which exposed them to the charge of corruption, and the military and the court circles did not accept that cabinets should be formed from the parliamentary majority. The earthquake of 1923 disrupted the economy, and the world slump after 1929 hit Japan’s export trade in silk and textiles, which removed the economic basis of the party cabinets. The response to the depression was reflation and, more importantly, the turn to the continent, since the army argued that expansion into Manchuria would solve the country’s problems of resources and markets.

learn.title: The seizure of Manchuria and the League

blocks.text: On 18 September 1931 officers of the Kwantung army staged an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway and used it as a pretext to occupy the province, acting without authorization from Tokyo and presenting the government with a fait accompli. Within months most of Manchuria was under Japanese control, and in 1932 the state of Manchukuo was proclaimed under the former Chinese emperor Puyi, a puppet administration that gave the occupation a constitutional form. During the operations the army bombarded Shanghai, which drew attention to the violence of the episode.

The League of Nations responded by sending the Lytton Commission, whose report concluded that Manchuria was not a case of Japanese self-defence and that Manchukuo lacked independence. Japan withdrew from the League in March 1933 as a result. The episode demonstrated the same weakness that the Abyssinian crisis would show in 1935: condemnation was possible, enforcement was not, and the power concerned could simply leave the institution that condemned it. Neither Britain nor the United States was prepared to use force, and the American Stimson doctrine of non-recognition changed no facts on the ground.

learn.title: Militarism and the road to the China war

blocks.text: The collapse of party government came through a combination of economic crisis and political violence. After the slump the cabinet of Inukai was replaced in 1932 by a cabinet of naval officers and then, in 1934, by a civilian government under Admiral Saito; party cabinets had ended. Officers of the young officers movement attempted coups in 1936, the February incident of that year in which cabinet ministers were assassinated before the revolt was suppressed, and the result was not a return to civilian politics but the army’s dominance over it. The control faction within the army, which favoured expansion on the continent rather than a northern war against the Soviet Union, set policy, and figures such as Tojo Hideki rose through the officer corps to the highest posts.

Japan left the League in 1933, signed the Anti-Comintern Pact with Germany in 1936 and withdrew from the naval treaties, so that by 1937 its foreign policy was unbound by any multilateral restraint. In July 1937 an incident at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing escalated into full-scale war, and Japanese forces took Beijing and Shanghai and advanced up the Yangtze, with Nanjing falling in December 1937 and atrocities accompanying the occupation. The war that followed was long and brutal, and it committed Japan to the continental commitments that would bring it into the wider conflict four years later.

questions.prompt: State four reasons for the growth of Japanese imperialism after 1919.
questions.answer: Four reasons are: the annexation of Korea in 1910 and the existing foothold in Manchuria through the South Manchuria Railway gave both a base and a direction for expansion; the refusal of the racial equality clause at the Paris conference convinced many that the western powers would not treat Japan as an equal; economic need, since resources and markets for silk and textile exports were sought on the continent, particularly after the slump of 1929; and the constitutional position of the army, which reported to the emperor and could force out civilian cabinets, allowed military leaders to pursue expansion against the government’s wishes. The twenty-one demands on China of 1915 are also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each reason must explain how it pushed Japan toward continental expansion.

questions.prompt: Explain why the League of Nations failed to stop the seizure of Manchuria.
questions.answer: Japan invaded in September 1931 and, as a founding member and a major power, it could not be compelled by an organisation that had no army of its own and required the cooperation of its members. The League responded by appointing the Lytton Commission, whose inquiry took most of a year, and by the time the report was published in 1932 Japanese control of Manchuria was an accomplished fact that the report declined to reverse, recommending only non-recognition of Manchukuo. Britain and the United States were unwilling to use force or to impose economic sanctions that might affect their own trade, and the American Stimson doctrine of non-recognition changed nothing on the ground. Japan’s response to the report was to withdraw from the League in March 1933, which showed that a member could leave without penalty. The lesson drawn by other powers facing aggression was that the League could condemn but not enforce, and the same pattern repeated over Abyssinia in 1935.
questions.explanation: The answer needs the mechanism: no enforcement power, great-power unwillingness, accomplished facts and costless withdrawal.

questions.prompt: Trace the establishment of militarism in Japan between 1932 and 1937.
questions.answer: Militarism replaced party government through a series of steps rather than a single coup. After the invasion of Manchuria in 1931, which the army had conducted on its own authority, the cabinet that followed in 1932 was formed of naval officers, and party cabinets never returned; a civilian admiral headed the government from 1934, with the parties marginalised. The turning point came in February 1936, when officers of the young officers movement assassinated cabinet ministers and senior figures before the revolt was suppressed; instead of restoring civilian authority the episode confirmed the army’s dominance over it, since the officers involved had drawn on the army’s grievance that the politicians had accepted reduction of the military budget. Abroad the consequences followed in sequence: Japan left the League of Nations in 1933 after the Lytton report, signed the Anti-Comintern Pact with Germany in 1936 and withdrew from the naval treaties, so that no multilateral constraint remained. In July 1937 the Marco Polo Bridge incident escalated into full-scale war in China, and the army’s dominance was confirmed by the conduct of a war that the civilian government had not planned. By 1937 therefore policy was set by a military leadership whose priorities came from the continent.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the domestic sequence and the foreign policy sequence linked together by the army’s constitutional position.

questions.prompt: Why did party government fail in Japan in the 1930s while it survived in Britain and the United States?
questions.answer: The first difference is constitutional. Japanese cabinets depended on the service ministers being serving officers, and the armed forces reported to the emperor rather than to the cabinet, so the army and navy could bring down a government at will by withdrawing their ministers. In Britain and the United States the military was subordinate to civilian authority by law and by convention, and no service chief could dismiss a government. The second difference is the depth of party politics. Party cabinets in Japan dated only from 1918 and rested on alliances with the bureaucracy, the zaibatsu and the court, while the parties themselves were exposed to corruption charges through zaibatsu funding; in Britain and the United States party government had developed over a century with mass membership and settled acceptance of its legitimacy. Third, the economic crisis struck at the base of Japanese party support: the slump hurt silk and textile exports and rural Japan severely, and the army offered a solution in continental expansion, whereas the depression in the western countries produced demands for reform within the system, the New Deal being the clearest example. Fourth, the political violence in Japan was met by a state that did not prosecute its authors decisively, while the western democracies contained equivalent extremism through established legal machinery. The result was that in Japan the military could present expansion as the answer to economic distress and act without authorization in Manchuria, then convert a successful fait accompli into political dominance, whereas in the west the same pressures were absorbed by parties and elections. The judgement is therefore that party government failed in Japan not because Japanese society lacked parties but because the constitutional structure gave the armed forces an unassailable lever and the economic crisis handed them the argument.
questions.explanation: Full marks need comparisons on the same basis, constitutional and economic, and an explicit judgement about which was decisive.
